messages.content: You are BioGPT, an expert compiler architect. Translate the provided natural language biological protocol into valid, deterministic BioScript code for execution on a microfluidic biochip.

ASSAY TYPE: Droplet-Based Digital Antibiotic Susceptibility (Minimum Inhibitory Concentration, MIC) Screen for Detecting Single-Cell Clonal Heteroresistance in an Isogenic Bacterial Population

REAGENTS USED:
  - Bacteria (Escherichia coli DH5-alpha carrying a TEM-20 beta-lactamase plasmid and a constitutively expressed YFP reporter plasmid, diluted to an encapsulation rate of ~0.1-0.3 bacteria per droplet)
  - Growth Medium (LB Lennox medium, co-encapsulated with the bacteria and antibiotic in each droplet)
  - Cefotaxime (beta-lactam antibiotic sodium salt; a separate droplet library is prepared for each concentration in a two-fold dilution series)

STEPS:
1. Droplet encapsulation: Using a flow-focusing microfluidic chip, an aqueous phase of bacteria, LB growth medium, and cefotaxime (at a fixed concentration for a given library) is encapsulated into monodisperse ~2 nL water-in-oil droplets stabilized by surfactant-stabilized fluorocarbon oil, forming a separate droplet library for each antibiotic concentration.
2. Dilution to single-cell occupancy: The starting bacterial suspension (~1x10^5 CFU/mL) is diluted so the average encapsulation rate (lambda) is ~0.1-0.3 bacteria per droplet, ensuring the vast majority of non-empty droplets contain only a single cell (~1,500 non-empty droplets screened per antibiotic concentration).
3. Off-chip incubation: Droplets are collected into a test tube and incubated off-chip overnight at 37 C, during which encapsulated bacteria proliferate and synthesize YFP unless growth is inhibited by the antibiotic.
4. Fluorescence detection: After incubation, each droplet is reintroduced to a microfluidic reading chip and its fluorescence is measured by confocal microscopy (488 nm excitation, 525/50 nm emission for YFP).
5. Digital growth classification: Each droplet's signal is compared against a fixed relative-fluorescence threshold (500) to classify it as growth-positive (1, strong fluorescence from a proliferated colony) or growth-negative (0, background fluorescence only, no proliferation).
6. Fraction/viability calculation: The fraction of positive droplets f+(c) is computed for each antibiotic concentration c and normalized by the positive fraction in the absence of antibiotic (f+(0)) to obtain single-cell viability F(c) = f+(c)/f+(0).
7. Repeat across concentration series: Steps 1-6 are repeated for a dilution series of cefotaxime concentrations (e.g., 16 two-fold dilutions in the virtual-array format, ranging from sub-inhibitory to fully inhibitory levels), each screened as an independent droplet library/measurement.
8. Disposal: After fluorescence readout, each analyzed droplet is discarded.

INTERPRETATION: The assay is digital and binary at the single-droplet level (grow/no-grow). Plotting viability F(c) against cefotaxime concentration and fitting with a Gompertz function yields the population MIC (concentration at 50% viability); the negative derivative of this fit gives the probability distribution p(MIC) of individual single-cell MICs, revealing clonal heteroresistance when the lowest concentration giving 100% inhibition is many-fold higher than the highest non-inhibitory concentration (heteroresistance was confirmed here, >8-fold). The same digital framework, combined with a colour-coded 'virtual array' of pooled dilutions, also allows precise measurement of the inoculum effect (MIC rising with bacterial density) and the amount of antibiotic per bacterium (MIA = MIC/N_CFU+), which remained stable (~0.5 ug/mL/CFU) across densities, supporting the method as a robust, high-throughput platform for characterizing heteroresistance and inoculum-density-resistant susceptibility testing.

module fluorescence

manifest Bacteria
manifest GrowthMedium
manifest Cefotaxime

instructions:

repeat 16 times {
    bacteria = dispense 1 units of Bacteria
    medium = dispense 1 units of GrowthMedium
    antibiotic = dispense 1 units of Cefotaxime

    a = mix bacteria with medium
    droplet = mix a with antibiotic for 5s

    heat droplet at 37c for 960m

    growth_signal = detect fluorescence on droplet for 30s

    if (growth_signal >= 500) {
        dispose droplet
    }

    dispose droplet
}

metadata.protocol_name: Droplet-Based Digital Antibiotic Susceptibility Screen Reveals Single-Cell Clonal Heteroresistance in an Isogenic Bacterial Population (Scheler, Makuch, Debski, Horka, Ruszczak, Pacocha, Sozanski, Smolander, Postek & Garstecki, Scientific Reports 2020)

sources.title: Droplet-based digital antibiotic susceptibility screen reveals single-cell clonal heteroresistance in an isogenic bacterial population

metadata.notes: The authored BioScript code is a direct translation of the paper's single-cell digital MIC assay workflow (Fig. 1A): co-encapsulation of a single bacterium, LB growth medium, and a fixed cefotaxime concentration into a water-in-oil droplet, overnight 37C incubation to allow proliferation and YFP synthesis, confocal fluorescence readout of the droplet, and a fixed-threshold (relative fluorescence 500, per Fig. 1B) binary classification into growth-positive/growth-negative before disposal. BioScript has no primitive for generating a population of thousands of parallel droplets per antibiotic concentration or for varying a numeric antibiotic concentration value across loop iterations, so the outer 'repeat 16 times' stands in for the paper's series of 16 two-fold cefotaxime dilutions (the virtual-array format, Fig. 2A) as 16 sequential single-droplet trials rather than a true parallel multi-thousand-droplet library per concentration. Likewise, because BioScript's grammar exposes only a 'detect fluorescence' primitive and not a generic optical/confocal detect module, 'detect fluorescence' is used directly here (unlike in the cortisol/DBS protocols, this matches the paper's actual YFP fluorescence readout rather than standing in for a different modality).

numeric_mismatches.note: The paper screens ~1,500 non-empty droplets per antibiotic concentration across up to 16 concentrations in a dilution series (and pools them into a colour-coded virtual array of ~22,000 droplets total). BioScript has no primitive for bulk/parallel droplet-population generation or per-droplet statistical aggregation, so this is approximated as 16 sequential single-droplet trials, one per concentration, rather than thousands of parallel replicate droplets per concentration.

numeric_mismatches.field: antibiotic held at a single fixed value across all 16 loop iterations
numeric_mismatches.note: The paper varies cefotaxime concentration in a two-fold dilution series across the 16 libraries (0.25 to 1024 ug/mL in the inoculum-effect experiment; 0 to ~0.91 ug/mL in the initial heteroresistance screen). BioScript's manifest/dispense model has no mechanism for varying a reagent's concentration value across repeat-loop iterations, so all 16 iterations dispense the same nominal 'Cefotaxime' unit amount rather than a true concentration gradient.

This numeric threshold is taken directly from the paper's stated relative-fluorescence cutoff for positive droplets (Fig. 1B), but the paper's actual classification also relies on population-level statistics (e.g., Poisson-based encapsulation-rate correction, f+(c)/f+(0) normalization) that are not modeled here.

numeric_mismatches.field: Gompertz-function MIC fitting, probability-distribution p(MIC) calculation, virtual-array colour-coding (Cascade Blue/Alexa 647), inoculum-effect (MIC vs N_CFU+) analysis, MIA/enzyme-degradation-rate estimation, bacterial clumping quantification
numeric_mismatches.note: Not modeled. These are downstream statistical/data-analysis, imaging-based clumping quantification, or virtual-array pooling procedures performed after droplet fluorescence acquisition, not part of the core droplet generation/incubation/detection/dispose cycle itself, and fall outside the scope of this translation.
